questions.q: A model's RMSE is much larger than its MAE on the same test set. What does that most likely indicate?
options: A few predictions have very large errors
The test set is too small
questions.explain: RMSE squares each error before averaging, so a handful of big misses pull it well above MAE. When the two are equal, all errors are about the same size.

questions.q: What R-squared does a model that always predicts the mean of the training target get, approximately?
questions.explain: R-squared compares your squared error with that of the mean predictor, so the mean predictor scores about 0. A model worse than the mean can score below 0.

questions.q: In cross_validate, why do you write scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error" and get negative numbers?
options: Because MAE can be negative for bad models
Because negative values are faster to compute
Because scikit-learn scorers always maximize, so errors are negated
questions.explain: Every scorer follows 'greater is better', so error metrics are negated. Multiply by -1 to report the usual positive MAE.

questions.q: A model's MAE grows from $16k on cheap homes to $44k on expensive ones, but its percentage error stays near 10% in every band. Which statement is right?
options: The model is broken on expensive homes
MAPE is wrong and should be ignored
The model is proportionally about equally accurate across price bands
questions.explain: Bigger prices naturally produce bigger dollar errors. A steady percentage error means the model is proportionally consistent, and the right metric depends on whether the business cares about dollars or percent.

questions.q: The same model scores R-squared 0.88 on the full test set but about -0.06 on only the mid-priced homes, with similar MAE. Why?
options: The model got worse on mid-priced homes
The metric has a bug for subsets
MAE hides the problem, so R-squared is the only reliable metric
R-squared depends on how spread out the target is in the data being scored
questions.explain: A narrow band has little variance to explain, so the same errors look large relative to it. Do not compare R-squared across different datasets or subsets.
